Jorge Luis Borges [@borges1941] imagined a garden where every possible outcome of every possible decision branches endlessly into parallel realities. Richard McElreath, in his excellent book "Statistical Rethinking" [@mcelreath2020], borrowed the image to make a point about statistics; to not be clever in the face of uncertainty, but thorough. To be thorough, one has to count all the ways the world could have produced what is being observed, and let the count inform the conclusion. This is less obvious when the link between what is observed and the target of inference is poorly understood; that is, when there are more possible paths than has been mapped.

![](book.png)

## An Underdetermined Ocean

The ocean reflects light in ways that carry, buried in their spectral shape, hints of the biological community it harbors. Diatoms, dinoflagellates, coccolithophores, each phytoplankton community leaves a faint optical fingerprint, and the ambition of ocean color remote sensing is to read that fingerprint from a distance and infer what is there. It's a great idea. It's also, in the technical sense, doubly underdetermined. The same spectrum can be produced by multiple different pigment assemblages. And a given pigment assemblage does not uniquely identify a community. The ambiguities in the two mappings, spectra to pigment assemblage and pigment assemblage to community structure, compound. These are not problems of measurement noise; they are structural features of the biology and physics involved. Moreover, photoacclimation means the same community can present different pigment signatures depending on its recent light history, and the pigment packaging effect means cell size modulates the absorption signal independent of community identity. The garden, in other words, has more forks than the fingerprint reveals.


## Don't Be Clever

This is where McElreath's injunction bites. Don't be clever. Don't commit to a single answer, as any point estimate model (gradient boosting, random forest, neural network) is forced to do by its own architecture. Count all the ways the data could have been produced and let the distribution speak. The ambiguity in the real ocean is not simply ignorance waiting to be cured by more data or better models. Much of it is structural, built into the physics and biology of the problem, and cannot be resolved by fitting a larger dataset. A model that produces a point estimate, this community at this confidence level, has no way to say "actually, several other communities are consistent with this spectrum to varying degrees."

![A single observed remote sensing reflectance spectrum (Rrs, center) forks outward through continuous layers of physical and biological ambiguity to a distribution of plausible community assemblages at the outer ring. Three illustrative optical regimes, pigment assemblages, and physiological states are shown, but the dashed concentric circles indicate that these represent samples from an underlying continuum of possibilities — any point on each circle is a plausible fork. Each outer-ring circle represents a member of a co-occurring assemblage, reflecting the reality that a given optical signal is consistent with multiple taxa present simultaneously in different proportions. The recurrence of the same taxon across paths originating from fundamentally different parts of the continuum illustrates the underdetermined nature of the Rrs-to-community inference problem: the same spectrum can be produced by, and is therefore consistent with, genuinely different community configurations.](forkingphyto.jpg){#fig-forking-phyto width="100%" .lightbox}

## Difficult, Difficult, Lemon-Difficult

To do the counting properly, to represent the full distribution over plausible community compositions given an observed spectrum, one needs a likelihood: a forward model from community to spectrum that is adequate to the biology, chemistry, and physics involved such that the resulting distribution is meaningful. Getting it right requires an explicit commitment to the biology, chemistry, and physics of the problem, one that cannot be quietly delegated to a loss function.

## The Heavy Burden of the Prior

In a problem where the data are sparse, the physics are ambiguous, and what we know about ecologically plausible community compositions in a given place and season is scientifically meaningful. This knowledge needs to be encoded, examined, and defended, not quietly absorbed into a model architecture. That is the role of the prior. That counting procedure, applied rigorously, is Bayes' theorem, not as one framework among many but as the uniquely correct way to update beliefs when reality is genuinely ambiguous. Pretending otherwise, which is what a purely data-driven approach does, is not neutrality. It is unexamined assumption disguised as objectivity.

This matters beyond the specific problem of phytoplankton community composition. Most algorithms in ocean remote sensing are evaluated, and implicitly legitimized, by frequentist metrics: R², RMSE, cross-validation scores. These metrics measure how well a model reproduces the data it was trained on. They say nothing about whether the model has correctly characterized the uncertainty in the underlying problem. In a genuinely underdetermined system, a model that produces a confident point estimate is a model that, by design, could very well fail to engage with a significant part of the problem. A Bayesian approach does not produce a single answer; it produces a distribution over all answers that are consistent with the data and prior knowledge, each weighted by its plausibility. That is what a posterior distribution is. That is what $R^2$ does not measure.

The argument here is not that Bayesian inference is always preferable; it is that for a specific class of problems, those where the underdetermination is real, the data are sparse, and prior knowledge is scientifically meaningful, frequentist metrics are the wrong measuring stick. They reward confidence. A Bayesian framework demands accounting.

## A Garden Among Gardens

The garden McElreath [-@mcelreath2020] describes, and the one illustrated earlier in this post, is nature's garden: all the ways the ocean could have produced the spectrum observed. Every fork in the tree is a physical or biological ambiguity that exists whether or not anyone is measuring it.

But nature's garden is not the only one in play. A second garden sits inside the first: the simulation. Real coincident measurements of ocean spectra and community composition are scarce, expensive, and sparse in space and time. A global coupled physical-biogeochemical model sidesteps this constraint elegantly. The NASA Ocean Biogeochemical Model coupled to the Ocean-Atmosphere Spectral Irradiance Model [@gregg2017] generates millions of paired observations cheaply, at any location and season, with full knowledge of the underlying community composition. It is an attractive solution, and the leap from there to training a machine learning model on the output and deploying it on real observations is a natural one. Such a model is not without value; Craig and Karaköylü [-@craig2025phyx] demonstrate precisely this point, showing that an XGBoost model trained on NOBM simulations can recover phytoplankton community composition from simulated satellite ocean color data with high skill. This constitutes a proof of concept that the signal is there to be found. The trouble is that the simulation, in generating all that tidy data, has already made choices. It assigns fixed optical properties to each phytoplankton group, represents photoacclimation through a handful of discrete states, and operates mostly in the open ocean where the coastal waters where biology gets complicated are excluded. These choices prune the forks. The simulation is not wrong; it represents real physics, but a narrow and tidy slice of it. It is nature's garden with most of the branches cut away. A machine learning model trained on it learns that tidy slice as if it were the whole garden, and the impressive performance metrics that follow are measuring performance within that pruned garden, not across the full one. The metrics are impressive because the problem was made easier before the model ever saw it.

A third garden, orthogonal to the first two, also needs consideration. This is the researcher's garden: the space of analytical decisions made before and after the model is built. Which simulation to trust. How to split training and test data. Which hyperparameters to tune. Which performance metrics to report and which to quietly set aside. This garden is not physical in that it does not exist in the ocean. Rather, it exists in the decisions, some conscious and some not, that determine what the model ever sees and how its performance is judged. Gelman and Loken [-@gelman2013garden] identified this garden in a different context, the replication crisis in psychology, but it grows just as readily in ocean remote sensing. A model that achieves an $R^2$ of 0.95 on held-out simulated data has found one path through this garden. Whether that path generalizes beyond the conditions the model was trained on is a question the metrics alone cannot answer.

The three gardens are not nested in any simple way. The simulation garden is a subset of nature's garden, just smaller. The researcher's garden is a different kind of thing entirely: epistemological rather than physical, a space of choices rather than phenomena. What connects them is interaction. The researcher's choices determine which slice of nature's garden the simulation represents. The simulation's choices determine what the model learns. And the model's reported performance is the leaf at the end of one particular path through all three gardens simultaneously.

The figure earlier in this post draws only the first garden. The dashed circles acknowledge that I am showing samples from a continuum rather than the continuum itself. The second garden is implied by what the figure leaves out. The third garden is the hardest to draw; not because it is more complex, but because it requires the researcher to turn the lens on themselves.
